tasks.description:
Rescue border collie mix, ~14 months. Pulls hard on leash, barks at every dog on walks. Fine in the house. South Bay CA, evenings and weekends. Wants: hire vs DIY, and a week-by-week plan.

=== ANSWER (full detail in attached report) ===

HIRE OR DIY? Both, split by capability not by topic.
- Leash pulling: DIY, fully.
- Enrichment/exercise restructure: DIY, fully — and it's the most urgent piece.
- Reactivity: DIY the foundation, but BUY structured help. Not for the information (that's free, and it's in the report) but because you cannot manufacture a cooperative trigger dog at a known distance on your own street. Controlled exposure is the scarce resource.

RECOMMENDED SPEND: ~$450-550. Equipment ~$150 + one six-week reactive class $300.

THE ANCHOR — and it's time-sensitive:
HSSV "Top Dogs" Level 1, six weeks online, $300, NEXT COHORT STARTS WED 19 AUG 2026 6:15PM (evening slot, fits availability). Humane Society Silicon Valley, 901 Ames Ave Milpitas, (408) 262-2133, dogtraining@hssv.org. Dogs 8mo+, no bite history — dog qualifies. Ask about the adopter discount. Level 2 ($300, in person) is the one with controlled real-dog exposure — that's the actual goal.
FREE FIRST STEP: hssv.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Reactive-Dog-Training-Guide-7.11.25.pdf

CORE PROTOCOL: Engage-Disengage. Stage 1 = mark and feed for looking at the trigger. Stage 2 = mark and feed for voluntarily looking back at you within a 3-count. Plus three emergency tools built in advance: U-turn, Find It, 1-2-3.
THE ONE TEST THAT MATTERS: if the dog won't take a high-value treat, you're too close. Add distance.

BIGGEST NON-OBVIOUS FINDING: this is less a training problem than an under-employed working dog. Threshold distance is not fixed — it shrinks when the dog is under-stimulated. Fixing enrichment buys threshold distance in DAYS; counter-conditioning takes MONTHS. Flirt pole + long-line sniff walks + retire the food bowl. Avoid the "just run it more" trap — cardio builds fitness and arousal without resolving the herding motor pattern.

EQUIPMENT: front/dual-clip harness (Blue-9 Balance or 2 Hounds Freedom) + DOUBLE-ENDED LEASH (the item people skip; it's the power steering) + biothane long line + treat pouch + flirt pole. ~$120-155. Measure chest girth first. No prong/choke/e-collar — AVSAB 2021 says no role for aversives in behavior modification, and for a reactive dog specifically they risk pairing pain with the sight of other dogs.

TIMELINE EXPECTATION: 8 weeks = foundation and visible progress, NOT a finished dog. Realistic horizon 3-6 months. Target is "notices a dog at 15 feet and looks back at me," not indifference. Measure threshold distance and RECOVERY TIME (improves first) — not reaction frequency, which improves last and will make you quit early.

=== STATE OF THE TREE ===
All 6 research subtasks DONE — findings written into their descriptions (reactivity protocol, equipment, enrichment, DIY-vs-pro + costs, local trainer shortlist with phone numbers, the 8-week plan).
9 human action subtasks created, all with contacts/prices/scripts already in them. Nothing further for the agent to do.
BLOCKING ITEM: HSSV registration, 19 Aug start. Everything else can slip.

report.markdown:
# Training Plan — 14-month Border Collie Mix, South Bay

## The short answer

**Do both — but not in the way most people split it.**

You have three separate problems that look like one:

| Problem | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Pulling on leash** | Fully DIY. Mechanical, well-documented, low risk. |
| **Barking/lunging at dogs** | This is *leash reactivity* — an emotional problem, not a manners problem. DIY the foundation, but buy structured help. |
| **Under-employed adolescent herding dog** | Fully DIY, and it's more urgent than either of the above. |

The reason to hire someone isn't the information — that's free and it's in this report. It's that **you cannot manufacture a cooperative trigger dog at a known distance in your own neighbourhood.** Other people's dogs won't hold position for you. That controlled exposure is the scarce resource, and it's what your money should buy.

**Recommended spend: ~$450–550.** Equipment (~$150) plus one six-week reactive-dog class ($300). That's it to start.

---

## The one time-sensitive thing

**Humane Society Silicon Valley runs "Top Dogs" — a three-level program built specifically for leash and barrier reactivity.** Next Level 1 cohort starts **Wednesday 19 August, 6:15pm**, online, six weeks, $300.

That timing is close to ideal: about two and a half weeks out, which gives you a runway to do the foundation work first and show up to class with a dog that will already take food outdoors.

- **Contact:** (408) 262-2133 · dogtraining@hssv.org · hssv.org/behavior-management-classes/
- **Eligibility:** dogs 8 months+, no bite history. Yours qualifies.
- **Ask about the adopter discount** — HSSV discounts classes for adopters, worth checking whether it extends to a dog adopted elsewhere.

**Why online isn't a downgrade:** you learn the handling mechanics at home with a calm dog, before asking the dog to perform them next to a trigger. Learning new timing while your dog is over threshold is precisely how people fail at this. Level 2 ($300, in person) is where the controlled real-dog exposure happens — that's the real prize, and it's what you're working toward.

There's also a **free Reactive Dog Training Guide PDF** from the same org. Read it before spending anything.

---

## What's actually going on with your dog

**"Reactive" is not "aggressive."** It's an over-reaction to a trigger, driven by emotion, and it comes in two flavours worth telling apart:

- **Frustration** — "I want to go say hi and this leash won't let me." Loose wiggly body, tail high, whining, straining *toward* the other dog. Extremely common in adolescent herding dogs who were friendly off-leash as puppies. Generally faster to resolve.
- **Fear** — "make it go away." Body low or stiff, hackles, hard stare, tries to retreat first.

There's a task in the tree for diagnosing which you've got, because it changes the emphasis.

**Two things about the timing are genuinely good news.** Fourteen months is peak adolescence, and reactivity emerging in this window is the single most common presentation there is. And the dog is fine in the house — this is situational, not a globally anxious dog.

**The concept everything hangs on is threshold.** Under threshold means far enough away that the dog notices the trigger but can still think, still take food, still hear you. The practical test is brutally simple: **if your dog won't take a high-value treat, you are too close.** Training only works under threshold. Every over-threshold explosion is a rep in the wrong direction.

One mechanical detail that explains a lot: on leash, the dog's flight option is removed. Fight/flight/freeze becomes fight/freeze. The same dog is calmer off-leash because it has somewhere to go.

---

## The part I'd push hardest on

**A 14-month border collie mix isn't primarily a training problem. It's an under-employed working dog.**

Threshold distance isn't a fixed property of your dog. It shrinks when the dog is under-stimulated, under-exercised or stress-stacked. Same dog copes at 40 feet on a good day and explodes at 10 feet on a bad one.

Which means: **fixing the enrichment gap buys you threshold distance in days.** The counter-conditioning takes months. If you only half-do one of the two halves of this plan, half-do the training and do the enrichment properly.

**The trap to avoid:** more running. Long repetitive cardio — especially chuck-it fetch to exhaustion — builds cardiovascular fitness so the dog needs more next month, and spikes arousal without ever resolving the herding motor pattern. Owner runs dog harder, dog gets fitter and more wired.

The herding sequence is eye → stalk → chase → grab. Ball-throwing exercises "chase" and leaves it hanging. What actually works:

- **Flirt pole** (~$25, or DIY from a horse lunge whip). Completes chase *and* capture. Five to ten minutes is genuinely tiring. Best effort-to-payoff ratio on the whole list.
- **Decompression sniff walks** on a long line, dog picks the route. Sniffing lowers heart rate and cortisol; East Bay SPCA calls these their number one recommendation for stressed dogs. Thirty minutes of sniffing beats thirty minutes of jogging for a reactive dog.
- **Retire the food bowl.** Puzzles, scatter feeding, snuffle mat. Every meal becomes a job, zero marginal effort once set up.
- **Ten minutes of trick shaping.** Costs nothing, works indoors, works when you're tired.

**Cut two things:** dog parks (uncontrolled greetings are how frustration-based reactivity gets worse), and 6pm neighbourhood sidewalk walks as the primary exercise — that's the highest-trigger, lowest-benefit hour of the day.

---

## Equipment

| Item | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Front/dual-clip harness | $33–50 | Blue-9 Balance (buckle-neck) or 2 Hounds Freedom No-Pull |
| **Double-ended leash** | $20–30 | **Don't skip this** — see below |
| Long line, 15–30ft biothane | $25–35 | Never retractable |
| Treat pouch | ~$15 | A fumbled treat is a lost rep |
| Flirt pole | ~$25 | Or DIY |
| **Total** | **~$120–155** | |

**The double-ended leash is the item people leave out and shouldn't.** Clip one end to the front ring, one to the back. It's power steering — you can turn the dog's front end away from a trigger without hauling on their neck, and it distributes the force. Karen Pryor's own shop recommends this pairing for strong pullers.

**Measure chest girth before ordering.** Both harnesses size by chest, not weight.

**A head halter (Gentle Leader, ~$25) is optional, not default.** Most control per pound of dog, but most dogs hate it initially and it needs a genuine one-to-two week desensitisation program. Only add it if harness plus double leash isn't enough to keep you safe.

### On prong and e-collars

Deliberately not on the list. AVSAB's 2021 position statement recommends reward-based methods only and states there is no role for aversive training in behavior modification plans, naming e-collars, prong collars, choke chains and leash corrections specifically.

Beyond the ethics, there's a mechanical reason it's a bad idea *for your dog in particular*: these tools deliver pain at the exact moment another dog appears. For a dog that already has a charged association with other dogs, you risk teaching "other dogs = pain." It often suppresses the barking while making the underlying emotion worse — and the classic outcome is a dog that stops giving warning signals and then bites without one. **Suppression is not resolution.**

If a trainer proposes one for the reactivity, that's a hard no.

---

## The core protocol: Engage–Disengage

One protocol, done consistently, beats four protocols done sloppily. This one works on both channels at once — changing how the dog *feels* and teaching it what to *do*.

**Stage 1 — Engage** (run for several days minimum)
1. Dog looks at the other dog → mark ("yes!") *as they look* → immediately feed.
2. Dog looks again → mark and feed again. Repeat.
3. If the dog ignores the marker or won't eat: **you're too close.** Add distance.

You're building: "other dog appears" reliably predicts "chicken appears."

**Stage 2 — Disengage** (only once Stage 1 is fluent)
1. Dog looks at trigger → you silently count to three.
2. Looks back at you before three → mark, feed. **This is the goal behavior.**
3. Doesn't look back → no problem, drop back to Stage 1.

**Three emergency tools to build first, in a boring place, before you need them:**
- **U-turn** — cue "let's go", turn, jog 10–20 feet, mark, feed.
- **Find It** — scatter treats on the ground, dog hoovers. Sniffing is self-calming.
- **1-2-3 treat** — rhythmic counting walk pattern, gives the dog something predictable.

**Trigger stacking is real.** Stresses accumulate. Three dogs in ten minutes and the third reaction is worse than the first at the same distance. After a bad encounter expect a lowered threshold for 24–72 hours. Plan a decompression day.

---

## The 8-week plan

Two tracks that never mix. **Track A** = leash mechanics, boring places, no dogs around. **Track B** = reactivity work, dogs present but far. Enrichment baseline runs underneath both from day one.

| Week | Track A — mechanics | Track B — reactivity |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Order gear. Read HSSV guide. Scout locations. | Film baseline. Diagnose fear vs frustration. Register for class. |
| **1** | Charge the marker indoors, 2×/day, 2 min. Build "Find It." | **Management only.** Cross the street, U-turn early. Goal is *zero* reactions via avoidance. |
| **2** | Build the U-turn — 20+ reps before you need it. 10-min training walks somewhere dull. Feed at your pant seam. | Still managing, not training. |
| **3** | Same, extend slightly. | **Find threshold.** Park at edge of a dog-frequented area. Start **Engage** only. 5–10 min, then leave. |
| **4** | 15-min walks, one mild distraction. | Consolidate Engage at the *same* distance. Don't close in yet. **Re-film and compare.** |
| **5** | Maintain. | Introduce **Disengage**. Start closing distance a few feet at a time. |
| **6** | Maintain. | Take it mobile — slow walk instead of stationary. Expect regression; drop back and rebuild. |
| **7** | Tracks begin to merge. | Generalise: 3 locations, varied trigger types. |
| **8** | — | **Re-film. Decision gate.** |

### Five rules that matter more than the schedule

1. **Under threshold or don't do it.** Dog won't take a treat = too close. That's the whole test.
2. **Sessions are 5–15 minutes.** Not 45. Short and frequent beats long and occasional.
3. **Cross the street. Leave. No ego.** Every explosion is a rep in the wrong direction.
4. **Separate the walk types** — training / decompression / potty — and use different gear for each so the dog can tell them apart. Trying to make one walk do all three jobs is why loose-leash training fails.
5. **Progress is not linear.** There will be a bad week. Bad weeks are data, not failure.

### The realistic daily version

**Bad day, 10 minutes** — scatter dinner in the grass, 10 min flirt pole, skip the walk. *A skipped walk is not a failed day. A walk where the dog rehearsed three explosions is.* Skipping is the better choice.

**Good day, 40 minutes** — 5 min trick warm-up indoors → 10 min Track A training walk → 20 min long-line sniff walk → 5 min settle with a chew.

---

## What the money buys

| Option | Cost |
|---|---|
| HSSV Top Dogs L1 / L2 / L3 (reactive, 6 wk each) | $300 each |
| Santa Clara Dog Training Club scentwork (5 wk) | $100 + $2.50 |
| Private session, South Bay | $95–120/hr |
| Reactive class elsewhere (comparison) | $275 East Bay SPCA · $400 Sonoma |
| Vet behaviorist initial consult (SF SPCA) | $595 |
| Vet-to-vet consult (specialist advises *your* vet) | from $150 |
| Full VB course, 3–6 months | $1,500–3,000 |

HSSV at $300 is mid-market and fair.

### Credentials, decoded

- **CBCC-KA** or **IAABC CDBC** — the advanced *behavior modification* credentials. **This is what matters for reactivity.**
- **CPDT-KA** — solid general trainer baseline, but general.
- **KPA-CTP** — strong hands-on, positive-reinforcement by design.
- **DACVB** — a veterinarian with behavior specialty. Can diagnose and prescribe. Top of the pyramid.

Verify anyone at `ccpdt.org/dog-owners/certified-dog-trainer-directory` or `iaabc.org/certs/members`.

### Red flags — walk away

- Proposes prong, choke, e-collar, or "leash corrections" for the reactivity
- Talks about dominance, alpha, pack leader, "your dog is testing you"
- **Guarantees** results
- Pushes **board-and-train** for reactivity — the dog returns to the same handler and street, and you learned nothing. This is handler training.
- Won't let you observe a class first
- Euphemisms: "balanced," "pressure," "e-touch," "stim"
- Pushes **flooding** — close-range exposure to "get them over it." Actively harmful.

**Also:** do not sneak a reactive dog into a standard manners class. Sirius Dog Training's own San Jose page says fearful or reactive dogs should do private lessons instead of their group class. That's normal and correct.

---

## Local shortlist

| Who | Where | Contact | For |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HSSV Top Dogs** | 901 Ames Ave, Milpitas | (408) 262-2133 · dogtraining@hssv.org | **First choice.** L1 online $300, L2 in person $300 |
| **South Bay Dog Training** | 186 E Sunnyoaks Ave Ste C, Campbell | (408) 429-8132 | Closest in-person reactive class, own facility. Pricing unpublished — call |
| **D For Dogz** (Kaajal) | Mobile, South Bay + Peninsula | (650) 538-3011 | "Growly Dog" class + private. Confirm evening slots |
| **Kuma Dog Training** | Mountain View | kumadogtraining.com | If you're northwest side |
| **Santa Clara Dog Training Club** | 344 Tully Rd, San Jose | santaclaradog.org | Scentwork $100/5wk — later, once foundation is in |
| **SF SPCA Vet Behavior** | SF | behaviorinfo@sfspca.org | Escalation only |
| **Bay Area Vet Behavior** (Dr. Sung, DACVB) | Walnut Creek | bayareavetbehavior.com | Escalation. CA telemedicine possible |

---

## Expectations, honestly

**Eight weeks gets you a foundation and visible progress. Not a finished dog.** Realistic horizon is three to six months, with some ongoing management for life.

The goal is not "dog no longer cares about other dogs." It's **"dog notices another dog at 15 feet and looks back at me instead of exploding."**

**Measure the right thing.** Reaction *frequency* is the last metric to improve, and judging by it will make you quit early. Track instead:

1. **Threshold distance** — is it shrinking?
2. **Recovery time** — how fast after a reaction can the dog take food again? **This improves first. It's your leading indicator.**
3. **Intensity** — a 3-second woof instead of a 20-second lunge?
4. **Voluntary check-ins** — is the dog looking back at you unprompted?

---

## Do these first

1. **Register for HSSV Top Dogs L1** — the 19 August cohort. Ask about the adopter discount. *Time-sensitive.*
2. **Download the free HSSV Reactive Dog Training Guide** — 20 minutes, costs nothing.
3. **Order equipment** — measure chest girth first.
4. **Film two walks** — baseline plus the fear-vs-frustration diagnosis.
5. **Mention the reactivity at your next vet visit** — pain lowers threshold, and a 14-month rescue of unknown breeding is squarely in the window for orthopaedic issues. Cheap to rule out, almost always skipped.

All nine action items are in the task tree with phone numbers, prices and scripts already in them.

tasks.description: We're shipping a consumer mobile app that scans a user's face to verify identity at signup, and we charge a monthly subscription. Before launch I need to know, state by state, which biometric privacy laws apply to us, what notice and written consent we have to collect, how long we're allowed to retain the scan, whether there's a private right of action, and what the penalties are. Flag the states that are genuinely dangerous to launch in.

comments.body:
Starting. Scoping this as: (1) dedicated biometric statutes with teeth — IL BIPA, TX CUBI, WA HB 1493; (2) comprehensive state privacy laws that treat biometrics as sensitive data requiring opt-in consent (~20 states); (3) sector/other laws that catch face scans (CO, CA CCPA/CPRA, NY C. 391-l, city ordinances like Portland/NYC); (4) a launch-risk ranking.

One thing worth flagging up front: because you charge a monthly subscription, Illinois BIPA is not your only Illinois problem — the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act plus auto-renewal law both bite. I'll cover BIPA in depth since it's the only statute with an unrestricted private right of action and it's what determines whether launch is viable.

I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice — the output is a research memo to brief outside counsel with, not a substitute for a review.
comments.author: agent

comments.body:
**Done — report attached. 10 research subtasks closed, 8 human subtasks queued.**

**The headline: there's no state you can't launch in.** Illinois is survivable and routinely survived — the companies losing BIPA cases collected first and papered later. What genuinely worries me isn't Illinois, it's three places where *no consent flow helps you* because they attack the product design rather than the disclosure:

- **Portland, OR** — an outright *ban*, whose definition of face recognition literally includes the word "verifying." $1,000 **per day** per violation plus fees, worse per-user than BIPA, and the "place or service" drafting plausibly reaches an app with no Portland presence. This was the biggest surprise in the research.
- **Colorado** — you may not refuse service to someone who declines the scan unless the biometric is *necessary*.
- **Maryland** — sensitive data only where *strictly necessary*, and **consent is expressly not a cure**.

**Two questions do most of the work, which is why they're the first two subtasks:**

1. **Is your verification legally required (KYC/AML/age) or a business choice?** One paragraph of work. A legal mandate likely unlocks Portland's "required by law" exception *and* strengthens Colorado and Maryland. Three problems, one answer.
2. **Do you qualify for BIPA's §25(c) GLBA exemption?** If yes, your largest exposure largely evaporates. *Cisneros v. Nuance* held an identity-verification provider **was** a financial institution because authenticating identity is a Fed-listed financial activity; *Davis v. Jumio* went the other way on a selfie-ID vendor. Genuinely unresolved and worth real legal spend.

**Two corrections to what you may be assuming:**
- You asked about retention limits per state. The better move is not to retain at all — "verify this person at signup" is *satisfied* the moment verification completes, and "purpose satisfied" is the operative trigger in IL, TX and CO alike. **Verify-and-discard removes most exposure everywhere.** I've made that an engineering decision subtask rather than burying it in a schedule.
- On your subscription: I checked whether charging money triggers BIPA §15(c)'s "profit from" ban. It doesn't — case law requires the biometric data itself to be transferred for value. But Colorado bars charging a *different* price to someone who declines biometric processing, so if you add an alternative verification path you can't price it differently.

**Two things I'd flag that you didn't ask about but that change the numbers:**
- **California's risk is a security problem, not a consent problem.** No PRA for ordinary processing, but the CCPA breach PRA covers biometric data at $100–$750 per consumer. A faceprint breach is a nine-figure event at scale.

report.markdown:
# Biometric Compliance for a Face-Scan Identity Verification App — 50-State Assessment

**Not legal advice.** This is a research memo to brief outside counsel with. Every "escalate to counsel" flag below is a real one.

---

## The short answer

**There is no state you cannot launch in.** Illinois is survivable and routinely survived — the companies losing BIPA cases are overwhelmingly those that collected biometrics first and papered the consent later. A correct consent flow is a near-complete defence in almost every state.

But three situations **cannot be fixed with better paperwork**, because they attack the product design rather than the disclosure:

| Problem | Where | Why paperwork doesn't fix it |
|---|---|---|
| A flat **ban** on face recognition | Portland, OR | No consent cures a prohibition |
| **"Necessary"** test for conditioning service on a scan | Colorado | We must prove the scan is necessary, not just disclosed |
| **"Strictly necessary"** test, consent expressly not a cure | Maryland | Consent is irrelevant by statute |

Those three need a **go/no-go decision**, not a compliance workstream.

### The two questions that change everything

1. **Is our verification legally required (KYC/AML/age) or a business choice?** A legal mandate likely unlocks Portland's "required by law" exception and greatly strengthens the Colorado and Maryland necessity arguments. One answer, three problems solved.
2. **Do we qualify for BIPA's §25(c) GLBA exemption?** If yes, our single largest exposure — Illinois — largely disappears. `Cisneros v. Nuance` held an identity-verification provider *was* a financial institution because authenticating identity is a Fed-listed financial activity. `Davis v. Jumio` went the other way on a selfie-ID vendor. Genuinely open, and worth real legal spend to resolve.

---

## The structural point most companies get wrong

There are **two layers** of law and they behave completely differently.

**Layer 1 — dedicated biometric statutes. No thresholds. Live from user one, day one.**
Illinois BIPA, Texas CUBI, Colorado HB 24-1130, Washington RCW 19.375, NYC's ordinance. Colorado *expressly removed* the Colorado Privacy Act's 100k/25k thresholds for biometrics.

**Layer 2 — comprehensive privacy laws. Mostly threshold-gated. Switch on as we grow.**
All 20 classify biometric data as sensitive data requiring opt-in consent.

> **You cannot phase biometric compliance in as you scale.** The consent flow, the written release and the public retention policy must be live at launch or you accrue liability with the first user.

**Sequencing:** at launch → BIPA, CUBI, CO, TX TDPSA, NE, NYC (+ WA MHMD if applicable). At ~35k users in a state → MD and RI. At ~100k or $25M revenue → essentially everything else. Thresholds count *per state*.

---

## Risk tiers

Ranked by expected cost of getting it wrong. The dominant variable is **private right of action with statutory damages and fee-shifting** — that is what funds a plaintiffs' bar that comes looking for you.

### Tier 1 — genuinely dangerous

**1. Illinois (BIPA, 740 ILCS 14).** The only unrestricted PRA. $1,000 negligent / $5,000 reckless per person, plus attorneys' fees, no injury required, 5-year limitations period (*Tims*).

*Good news:* SB 2979 (Aug 2024) overrode *Cothron*'s per-scan accrual — repeat collection of the same biometric from the same person by the same method is now **one violation, one recovery**, and the Seventh Circuit has held this retroactive. The same amendment made **electronic signature** valid for a written release, which is what makes an in-app flow viable at all.

*Sober news:* 100+ BIPA class actions were filed in 2025. Of a tracked sample of 182 suits, 51 concerned facial geometry and 35 of those targeted smartphone apps. Identity verification for app users is a named category of defendant. **This is our exact fact pattern.** Model at **$200–$550 per Illinois user** based on observed settlements (Pret A Manger ≈$518/member; Clearview $51.75M; a 150k-member facial recognition class at $47.5M).

*The photograph exclusion will not save us* — *Rivera v. Google* rejected the argument that templates derived from photos fall in the exception.

**2. Portland, OR (City Code ch. 34.10).** Ranked this high despite being one city.

- It is a **ban**, not a consent regime.
- The definition of face recognition technology expressly includes **"verifying"** — that is our product named in the statute.
- "Places of public accommodation" means "any place **or service**" — practitioners read this as plausibly reaching online services with **no Portland presence**.
- **$1,000 per day, per violation**, plus attorneys' fees. Per-day accrual is worse than BIPA, which has no daily multiplier.
- Exceptions: compliance with law (**our best hope**); user verification to unlock *the user's own device* (not us — this is Face ID, not server-side verification); social media face detection (not us).

**3. Texas (CUBI, Bus. & Com. Code ch. 503).** No PRA, but the Texas AG has produced the two largest privacy settlements in US history under this statute: **$1.4B (Meta, 2024)** and **~$1.375B (Google, 2025)**. $25,000 per violation, counted per capture *and* per disclosure. No revenue or headcount threshold. Enforcement targets high-volume consumer-facing biometric capture.

Two notes: CUBI does **not** require a signed written release (informed consent suffices), so a BIPA-grade flow over-satisfies it. But CUBI has **no photograph exclusion**, making it broader than BIPA in that respect, and its only carve-out is for *voiceprints* held by financial institutions — narrower than BIPA's §25(c) and no help to us.

### Tier 2 — serious, manageable

**4. Washington (My Health My Data).** The only other PRA, via the Consumer Protection Act. Blunted by the need to prove injury to business or property and no statutory damages. Open question: MHMD lists "biometric data" in its definition of health status, but the chapeau requires data identifying *health status* — an ID faceprint reveals none. Untested; first class action filed Feb 2025 on exactly this theory. There is a strong fraud-prevention exception argument.

*Separately, RCW 19.375 (HB 1493) probably does not apply to us at all* — it excludes photographs, video, "**or data generated therefrom**," which is far broader than BIPA's exclusion, and its "security purpose" definition expressly covers protecting the integrity of accounts and online services.

**5. Colorado (HB 24-1130, in force 1 July 2025).** No PRA; $20,000 per violation; AG and DAs. Applies at any volume. Elevated because of the **conditioning prohibition** — we may not refuse service to someone who declines the scan unless the biometric is *necessary*, and we may not charge them differently (relevant to a subscription).

**6. Maryland (MODPA).** Modest penalties, no PRA — but **consent is not a cure**. Sensitive data may only be processed where *strictly necessary* to provide the requested service, and the term is undefined with no guidance yet. The question commentators keep asking is precisely ours: is a face scan strictly necessary when document upload would work?

**7. California.** Ordinary processing is regulator-enforced, no PRA — **but the CCPA breach PRA covers biometric data** at $100–$750 per consumer per incident. California risk is therefore a function of our **security** posture, not our consent posture. A faceprint breach is a nine-figure event at scale.

### Tier 3 — overhead, not existential

**8. NYC** — PRA exists, but "commercial establishment" (places of entertainment, retail, food and drink) probably excludes a pure app. Signage violations carry a 30-day cure; **selling biometrics has no cure period at all**. Never monetise faceprints.

**9. The remaining comprehensive-law states** (VA, CT, OR, NJ, DE, NH, MN, NE, IN, KY, RI, IA, MT, FL, TN, UT) — opt-in consent, DPIAs, consumer rights, ~$7,500/violation, no PRA. One good flow satisfies all. UT and TN are least demanding ($25M revenue floors). TX TDPSA and NE have **no threshold at all**.

**10. The ~25 states with neither law** — residual exposure is UDAP/deceptive practices. Practical rule: don't say anything in the privacy policy that isn't true.

---

## Retention: one national rule, not fifty

Deadlines conflict — TX 1 year after purpose expires, CO 24 months after last interaction, IL 3 years. Don't build per-state logic. Build the strictest:

1. **Delete the raw capture within 24 hours** of template generation (hard ceiling 7 days). No state requires keeping it; keeping it makes every case worse. **Highest-value single change available.**
2. **Delete the template on successful verification.** "Verify this person at signup" is *satisfied* the moment verification completes — and "purpose satisfied" is the operative trigger in IL, TX and CO alike. A verify-and-discard product has almost no retention exposure anywhere. **This is the recommended architecture.**
3. **If we must retain:** earliest of purpose satisfied / **12 months** after last interaction / 30 days after cancellation. 12 months sits inside Texas's rule with margin and automatically satisfies CO and IL.
4. **Keep a non-biometric artifact instead** — a boolean "verified", date, method, consent record. Preserves the audit trail without the regulated data.
5. **Deletion must reach backups and vendors.** MHMD extends deletion to backups. Our deletion is meaningless if the vendor's doesn't happen.
6. **Annual documented review** (Colorado requires it; the record *is* the compliance artifact).
7. **Publish the schedule before collecting anything** — see below.

---

## What must be true before launch

**Consent screen**
- Its own screen, before the camera ever activates — gated on a returned consent token. Pre-consent capture is the most common BIPA fact pattern.
- Not bundled into the ToS. Colorado states expressly that blanket ToS acceptance is not consent.
- No pre-ticked boxes, no dark patterns, accept and decline of equal visual weight.
- Separate consent for third-party disclosure.

**Four mandatory disclosures** (BIPA §15(b) + CO): that a biometric is being collected and stored, in plain words; the **specific** purpose; the **specific** storage term (not "as long as necessary"); named third-party recipients.

**Evidence to store:** user ID, UTC timestamp, notice **version ID** and text hash, app version, affirmative action taken. Version every change and keep all prior versions — BIPA's limitations period is 5 years, so **consent records must outlive the biometric data**. Log deletion events too; proving destruction matters as much as proving consent.

**Published before first scan:** the public retention & destruction policy. BIPA §15(a) and Colorado both require it, and *Mora v. J&M Plating* holds it must exist **upon possession** — publishing later does not cure earlier users. Do not publish a policy the product doesn't actually follow; that converts a privacy claim into a deceptive-practices claim.

**Acceptance test:** a tester in Illinois must see the notice before the camera turns on, read all four disclosures, be able to decline, and afterwards have a retrievable record of the exact text and timestamp. If any of that fails, we are not ready to launch in Illinois.

---

## Recommendations

1. **Answer the "legally required?" question first.** It's one paragraph of work and it unlocks Portland, Colorado and Maryland simultaneously.
2. **Pursue the GLBA exemption analysis.** Highest return on legal spend available.
3. **Build verify-and-discard.** Most retention risk is architectural, not legal.
4. **Offer a non-biometric alternative path.** Resolves Colorado's conditioning problem, strengthens Maryland, avoids geofencing. Counter-argument worth weighing with counsel: offering it is evidence the scan was never "necessary." On balance still the safer design. If we offer it, we cannot charge those users more in Colorado.
5. **Ask counsel about arbitration with a class-action waiver.** It is the one lever that changes Illinois exposure more than any amount of compliance work. A real business decision with real downsides — but it belongs on the table.
6. **Build to the strictest common denominator once and ship it in all 50 states.** Maintaining 20 divergent consent configurations costs more than over-complying, and the thresholds move every session.

---

## Watch list

New York (a BIPA-style bill with a PRA keeps being introduced — **the largest single adverse change possible for us**); Maryland AG guidance defining "strictly necessary"; Washington rulings on biometrics as consumer health data; the Seventh Circuit in *Cisneros* on §25(c); Colorado SB 24-205's moving effective date; Texas HB 149 (TRAIGA, effective 1 Jan 2026, relevant if we ever train models on collected face data).

tasks.title: Research: what leash reactivity actually is and the standard protocol
tasks.description:
FINDINGS — leash reactivity: what it is and the standard protocol

WHAT IT IS
"Reactive" is not aggressive. It's an over-reaction (bark/lunge/spin) to a trigger, driven by emotion — usually one of two flavors:
- FRUSTRATION / barrier-frustration ("I want to go say hi and this leash won't let me"). Very common in adolescent herding dogs who were friendly off-leash as puppies. Dog is often loose-bodied, whining, tail high/wagging.
- FEAR ("make it go away"). Body low or stiff, hackles, hard stare, retreat attempts.
Key mechanic behind both: on leash the dog's flight option is removed. Fight/flight/freeze becomes fight/freeze, so leashed dogs run hotter than the same dog off-leash. (Pet Professional Guild.)
=> WORTH IDENTIFYING WHICH ONE. Frustration-type generally resolves faster. See human subtask "Film two walks and identify frustration vs fear."

THRESHOLD — the single most important concept
"Under threshold" = far enough from the trigger that the dog notices it but can still think, still take food, still respond to you. Practical definition used by CBCC-KA trainers: any behavior that is NOT lunging/barking counts as under threshold. If your dog ignores a high-value treat, you are too close. Full stop — that's the test.
Training only works under threshold. Every over-threshold rehearsal is practice at being reactive and sets you back.

THE CORE PROTOCOL — Engage-Disengage (Preventive Vet / Cathy Madson CBCC-KA; also on Karen Pryor Clicker Training)
Works on both classical (change the feeling) and operant (teach a behavior) channels at once. Two stages:

Stage 1 — ENGAGE (run for several days minimum before moving on)
- Dog looks at the trigger → mark ("yes!" or click) AS they look → immediately feed, encouraging head turn back to you.
- Dog looks at trigger again → mark and feed again. Repeat.
- If dog ignores the marker or won't take the treat: you are too close. Add distance.
- What you're building: "other dog appears" reliably predicts "chicken appears."

Stage 2 — DISENGAGE (reinforcing the dog's OWN choice to look away)
- Dog looks at trigger → you silently count to three.
- Looks back at you before 3 → mark and feed. This is the goal behavior.
- Doesn't look back by 3 → no problem, just do Stage 1 (mark for looking). Also a signal you may be too close or not ready for stage 2.

OTHER NAMED PROTOCOLS (same underlying principles, pick one and be consistent)
- LAT / "Look At That" — Leslie McDevitt, from Control Unleashed. Essentially Engage with a cue attached; you can eventually ask for it.
- BAT 2.0 — Grisha Stewart. Uses long line, dog moves itself away from trigger; the reinforcer is distance/relief rather than food. Better for fear-based; needs more space and set-ups with a helper dog. Harder to DIY.
- Pattern games (McDevitt) — "1-2-3 treat", "Find It" scatter. Not counter-conditioning per se; these are the EMERGENCY TOOLS for when a dog appears too close and you need to get past. Underrated, easiest to learn.
RECOMMENDATION: Engage-Disengage as the main protocol + "Find It" and "1-2-3" as emergency escape hatches + a trained U-turn ("let's go"). Skip BAT unless a trainer runs it for you.

SUPPORTING PIECES
- Trained U-turn: cue "let's go", turn and jog 10-20 feet, then mark and feed. Build it in a boring environment BEFORE you need it. Recommended as standard equipment for every reactive-dog walk (Pet Professional Guild).
- Trigger stacking: stresses accumulate. Three dogs in ten minutes = the third reaction is worse than the first even at the same distance. After a bad encounter, expect a lower threshold for ~24-72h. Plan a decompression day.

REALISTIC TIMELINE
No credible source promises a fix in weeks. Expect meaningful improvement over 3-6 months of consistent short sessions; ongoing management for life in some form. The realistic goal is NOT "dog no longer cares about other dogs" — it's "dog can notice another dog at 15 feet and look back at me instead of exploding." 8 weeks gets you the foundation and visible progress, not a finished dog. Set expectations accordingly.

tasks.title: Research: loose-leash walking mechanics and equipment
tasks.description:
FINDINGS — loose-leash mechanics and equipment

THE AVERSIVE-TOOL QUESTION (answer this before buying anything)
AVSAB (American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior) 2021 Humane Dog Training position statement: reward-based methods only, for all aspects of training and behavior modification. It explicitly names electronic collars, prong collars, choke chains and leash corrections as aversive methods to avoid, and states there is no role for aversive training in behavior modification plans — no exceptions.
Why this matters SPECIFICALLY for your dog, beyond ethics: a prong or e-collar delivers pain at the exact moment another dog appears. For a dog who already has a negative or over-aroused association with other dogs, you risk teaching "other dogs = pain." It can suppress the barking while making the underlying emotion worse — the classic outcome is a dog that stops giving warning signals and then bites without one. Suppression is not resolution.
=> If a trainer proposes a prong or e-collar for the reactivity, that's a hard no. See the DIY-vs-pro subtask for the full red-flag list.

EQUIPMENT — recommended setup
1. FRONT-CLIP / DUAL-CLIP HARNESS (primary recommendation)
   - Blue-9 Balance Harness (buckle-neck version) — 6 points of adjustment, 2 D-rings (front + back), no-choke/no-chafe, doesn't restrict shoulder movement. Widely recommended by force-free trainers; sold through Karen Pryor's own shop. ~$40-50. Buckle-neck version means you don't have to push it over the head — useful for a dog that's head-shy.
   - 2 Hounds Design Freedom No-Pull Harness — the other standard recommendation. Front + back rings, martingale loop on the back that tightens gently across the chest. ~$33-39 depending on size/retailer (Mud Bay lists $32.99-38.99; 2houndsdesign.com from $32.98).
   Either is fine. Balance if you want max adjustability, Freedom if you want the martingale action.

2. DOUBLE-ENDED LEASH (this is the part people skip and it's the highest-leverage purchase)
   Clip one end to the front ring, one to the back ring. Gives you power-steering — you can turn the dog's front end away from a trigger without hauling on their neck, and it distributes force. Karen Pryor's shop specifically suggests a double-ended leash with the Balance Harness for strong pullers. ~$20-30. Blue-9 makes one; any 6ft double-clip training lead works.

3. LONG LINE, 15-30ft, biothane (NOT retractable)
   For decompression/sniff walks in open low-traffic space. ~$25-35. Biothane over nylon: doesn't hold water, doesn't give rope burn.

4. HEAD HALTER (Gentle Leader / Halti) — conditional, not default
   Most physical control per pound of dog; PetSafe Gentle Leader is veterinary-behaviorist designed. BUT: most dogs hate it initially and it needs a genuine 1-2 week desensitization program (treat for nose-in, build duration, never let the dog hit the end of the leash hard — risk of neck torque). ~$20-27.
   Verdict: only add this if the harness + double-ended leash genuinely isn't enough to keep the dog safe, and if you're willing to do the conditioning. Don't slap it on and walk out the door.

5. TREAT POUCH + high-value food
   Non-negotiable. Real food, not kibble, not dry biscuits: string cheese, turkey hot dog, chicken, freeze-dried liver. Soft and smelly so it's fast to eat and worth working for. A fumbled treat delivery is a lost rep. ~$15 pouch.

APPROXIMATE STARTER SPEND: $110-160 for harness + double-ended leash + long line + pouch. Head halter adds ~$25.

MECHANICS — why the pulling happens and how to fix it
- Pulling is self-reinforcing: dog pulls, dog gets to the interesting smell, pulling worked. Every walk where pulling gets the dog forward is a training session in favor of pulling.
- Core rule: forward motion is the reward. Leash goes tight → you stop moving or reverse. Leash is loose → walking continues. Be a tree / penalty yards. Boring but it's the actual mechanism.
- Reinforce in position: feed at your pant seam, repeatedly, while the dog is where you want them. Most owners only respond to the dog when it's wrong. Pay heavily for correct position early.
- SEPARATE THE WALK TYPES. This is the fix that makes everything else possible:
  * TRAINING walk — short (10-15 min), harness front clip, high rate of reinforcement, criteria enforced.
  * DECOMPRESSION / sniff walk — long line, dog chooses the route, sniffing is the point, zero manners criteria. Sniffing is documented to lower heart rate and cortisol; East Bay SPCA calls decompression walks their number one recommendation. This is where the dog's actual exercise and stress-relief needs get met.
  * POTTY walk — get out, get it done, no expectations.
  Trying to make one walk do all three jobs is why loose-leash training fails. Use different equipment for each so the dog can tell them apart.

tasks.title: Research: exercise and mental-work needs for an adolescent border collie mix
tasks.description:
FINDINGS — exercise and mental work for a 14-month border collie mix

WHY THIS BRANCH MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE TRAINING
An under-stimulated herding adolescent walks around with a permanently elevated baseline arousal. Threshold distance is not a fixed property of the dog — it shrinks when the dog is under-exercised, under-stimulated or stress-stacked. Meaning: the same dog reacts at 40 feet on a bad day and 10 feet on a good one. Fixing the enrichment gap is the cheapest way to buy yourself threshold distance, and it works within days, unlike the counter-conditioning which takes months.
Do not treat this as optional or "nice to have." For this breed and age it is load-bearing.

THE BREED LOAD
General guidance for border collies is roughly 2 hours of activity a day, split across the day rather than in one block (Dogster, vet-reviewed; Hepper, vet-approved). A mix may need less than a pure working-line collie, but plan for a lot.
CRITICAL CAVEAT — you cannot meet this with running alone. Long repetitive cardio (especially chuck-it fetch to exhaustion) builds cardiovascular fitness, so the dog needs more next month, and it spikes arousal without ever resolving the herding motor pattern. This is the classic trap: owner runs the dog harder, dog gets fitter and more wired.

WHAT ACTUALLY SATISFIES A HERDING DOG
The herding sequence is eye → stalk → chase → grab. Repetitive ball-throwing only exercises "chase" and leaves it unresolved. Options that complete the sequence or substitute for it:
- FLIRT POLE — lunge whip + rope + toy. Completes chase AND capture, so the dog gets resolution. 5-10 minutes is genuinely tiring. ~$25, or DIY from a horse lunge whip. Best effort-to-payoff ratio on this whole list. Rules: let the dog win regularly, keep turns short, don't do sharp turns on a growing dog's joints.
- HERDING BALL / TREIBBALL — dog pushes a large ball. Urban herding. Satisfies the push-and-control urge.
- SNIFFING / DECOMPRESSION WALKS — long line, dog picks the route. Sniffing lowers heart rate and cortisol; East Bay SPCA names decompression walks their number one recommendation for stressed dogs. 30 min of sniffing beats 30 min of jogging for a reactive dog, every time.
- SCENT WORK / NOSEWORK — the single best formal outlet for a reactive dog because dogs work one at a time and the format is naturally distanced. Also builds confidence. See local options below.
- TRICK TRAINING / SHAPING — 10 minutes of free-shaping a new trick genuinely takes the edge off a collie. Costs nothing, works indoors, works in bad weather, works when you're tired.
- FOOD PUZZLES / SCATTER FEEDING / SNUFFLE MAT — stop using a bowl. Every meal becomes a job. Zero marginal effort once set up.

LOCAL FORMAL OUTLETS (South Bay)
- Santa Clara Dog Training Club — 344 Tully Rd, San Jose. Scentwork classes $100 + $2.50 registration for a 5-week session, Tuesdays. Classes start every 7 weeks. Also obedience, rally, tricks. Website: santaclaradog.org/classes. NOTE: scentwork has a prerequisite — proficiency in Beginner Obedience or CGC-ready. Cheapest structured enrichment found by a wide margin.
- Orion Dog Training — nose work class, 576 E Santa Clara St, San Jose. Six-week ongoing format. oriondogtraining.com.
DEFER these until after the reactivity foundation is in — group settings are hard for a reactive dog. Good week 8+ goal. Scent work is the right FIRST sport because of the one-dog-at-a-time format.

THE REALISTIC DAILY BUDGET (for an evenings-and-weekends owner)
Weekday, ~45-55 min total, none of it heroic:
- Breakfast out of a puzzle or scattered in grass (0 min of your time)
- 10-15 min flirt pole or backyard training game
- 20-30 min decompression sniff walk on the long line in a low-traffic spot
- 5-10 min trick/shaping session in the living room
- Evening chew or lick mat while you eat dinner
Weekend: add one longer outing — a hike, a Sniffspot rental (private fenced yards, bookable by the hour, genuinely useful for reactive dogs because you get space with no other dogs), or a quiet trail at an off-peak hour.

WHAT TO CUT
- Dog parks. Full stop, for this dog. Uncontrolled greetings with over-aroused dogs are how frustration-based leash reactivity gets worse.
- Busy neighborhood sidewalk walks at 6pm as the only form of exercise. That is the highest-trigger, lowest-benefit hour of the day. Shift walks earlier or later, or drive somewhere quieter.

tasks.title: Research: DIY vs hire a pro — decision criteria and what pros cost in the South Bay
tasks.description:
FINDINGS — DIY vs hire a pro, and what pros cost in the South Bay

THE HONEST ANSWER: SPLIT IT. Different parts of this problem have different answers.

| Piece | DIY? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Leash pulling / loose-leash walking | YES, fully | Mechanical, well documented, low risk of making it worse |
| Enrichment + exercise restructure | YES, fully | Just needs doing |
| Emergency tools (U-turn, Find It, 1-2-3) | YES, fully | Simple, and you'll learn them fastest by just doing them |
| Counter-conditioning the reactivity | YES to start, BUT | DIY-able in principle; the hard parts are (a) reading threshold correctly and (b) getting controlled set-ups. A stranger's dog will not cooperate with your training plan |
| Assessing fear vs frustration, and prognosis | NO — get eyes on it | 20 minutes of a pro watching you walk is worth weeks of guessing |
| Any bite history, or reaction that includes people/children | NO — pro immediately | Out of scope for self-teaching |

RECOMMENDED SHAPE: DIY the foundation for 2-3 weeks, and in parallel book ONE structured intervention — ideally a dedicated reactive-dog class, which is dramatically better value than private sessions for this specific problem. The reason: a reactive-dog class gives you what you cannot manufacture on your own — other dogs at a controlled, known distance, handled by people who will actually hold position when you need them to. That's the scarce resource, not the information.

STRONGEST SIGNALS YOU SHOULD STOP DIY AND CALL SOMEONE
- Any bite, or teeth-on-skin contact, with a dog or a person
- Reactivity generalizing (started with dogs, now includes bikes/kids/skateboards)
- Redirected aggression — dog bites the leash, or you, when frustrated
- You're getting hurt, or afraid to walk the dog
- Eight weeks of consistent work with zero change
- You've started dreading walks / avoiding them entirely (avoidance makes it worse and it's a quality-of-life issue for you)

CREDENTIALS — decoded
- CPDT-KA — Certified Professional Dog Trainer, Knowledge Assessed (CCPDT). The baseline general credential. Requires exam + logged hours + continuing education.
- CPDT-KSA — as above plus a hands-on skills assessment. Rarer.
- CBCC-KA — Certified Behavior Consultant Canine, Knowledge Assessed (CCPDT). ADVANCED, specifically for behavior modification. Covers applied behavior analysis, ethology, body language. THIS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS FOR REACTIVITY.
- KPA-CTP — Karen Pryor Academy Certified Training Partner. Strong hands-on program, positive-reinforcement by design.
- IAABC CDBC — Certified Dog Behavior Consultant. Also advanced behavior work, case-study based. Equally good signal as CBCC-KA.
- DACVB — Diplomate, American College of Veterinary Behaviorists. A VETERINARIAN with behavior specialty. Can diagnose, can prescribe medication. Top of the pyramid.
- Fear Free Certified — handling-focused, nice-to-have, not sufficient alone.
- No credential at all / "20 years experience" / "balanced trainer" / "pack leader" / "dominance" / "alpha" — not a credential. See red flags.
Directories to verify anyone in: ccpdt.org/dog-owners/certified-dog-trainer-directory, iaabc.org/certs/members, karenpryoracademy.com/find-a-trainer.

RED FLAGS — walk away
- Proposes a prong collar, choke chain, e-collar/shock collar, or "leash corrections" for the reactivity. AVSAB's 2021 position statement is explicit that these are aversive and that there is no role for aversive training in behavior modification plans — no exceptions. For a reactive dog specifically, this risks pairing pain with the sight of other dogs.
- Talks about dominance, alpha, pack leader, or "your dog is testing you."
- GUARANTEES results. Nobody credible guarantees behavior.
- Board-and-train for reactivity. The dog comes back to the same handler, same street, same triggers, and you learned nothing. Reactivity work is handler training. Avoid.
- Won't let you watch a class before enrolling.
- Vague about methods, or uses euphemisms ("pressure", "corrections", "e-touch", "stim", "balanced").
- Pushes flooding — deliberately exposing the dog to triggers at close range to "get them over it." Actively harmful.

WHAT IT COSTS — South Bay benchmarks (verified, mid-2026)
| Option | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| HSSV Top Dogs L1 (reactive, online, 6 wk) | $300 | Adopter discount may apply |
| HSSV Top Dogs L2 (reactive, IN PERSON, 6 wk) | $300 | Requires L1 |
| HSSV Top Dogs L3 (topics/sports, 6 wk) | $300 | Requires L1+L2 |
| HSSV general Manners class (6 sessions) | $200 | Not for reactive dogs |
| HSSV Sports classes | $225 | |
| Santa Clara Dog Training Club scentwork (5 wk) | $100 + $2.50 reg | Cheapest structured option anywhere |
| Private session, generic US range | $75-$120/hr | Typical band |
| Private session, San Jose (Dog Academy listing) | from $95 | |
| Reactive-dog group class, other Bay Area shelters (comparison) | $275 (East Bay SPCA, 5wk) / $400 (Humane Soc. Sonoma Cty, 75min/wk) | HSSV at $300 is mid-market and reasonable |
| Veterinary behaviorist initial consult (SF SPCA) | $595 | Includes assessment, diagnosis, plan, follow-up support |
| Vet-to-vet consult (SF SPCA) | from $150 | Cheap route to specialist input via your own vet |
| Full VB treatment course, 3-6 months | $1,500-$3,000 | Declines over time as visits space out |

BUDGET GUIDANCE — three tiers
- LEAN (~$150-250): equipment only + free HSSV Reactive Dog Training Guide + DIY. Legitimate starting point given the dog has no bite history.
- RECOMMENDED (~$450-550): equipment (~$150) + HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 ($300). Best value on the board.
- IF IT STALLS (+$400-700): add 2-3 private sessions with a CBCC-KA/CDBC trainer, or Top Dogs Level 2 in person.
- ESCALATE (+$595): veterinary behaviorist, if there's a bite, if anxiety looks generalized beyond walks, or if medication is worth evaluating. Note a VB can prescribe — for genuinely fear-based cases medication isn't failure, it's what makes the training possible.

ONE MORE THING WORTH KNOWING
Sirius Dog Training's own San Jose class page states that fearful or reactive dogs should do private lessons with an experienced trainer rather than joining their general group class. This is normal and correct — do NOT try to sneak a reactive dog into a standard manners class. It will go badly, you'll be embarrassed, and the dog will rehearse reacting for an hour. Reactive dogs need reactive-dog-specific classes.

tasks.title: Write the week-by-week training plan
tasks.description:
THE 8-WEEK PLAN (full version is in the report attached to the parent task t-dog)

STRUCTURE: two parallel tracks that never mix.
- TRACK A — Leash mechanics. Boring, quiet places, no other dogs present. Front-clip harness + double-ended leash.
- TRACK B — Reactivity / Engage-Disengage. Other dogs present but FAR. Only ever under threshold.
Plus a non-negotiable enrichment baseline underneath both.

THE FIVE RULES THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE SCHEDULE
1. Under threshold or don't do it. Dog won't take a treat = too close. That's the whole test.
2. Sessions are 5-15 minutes. Not 45. Short and frequent beats long and occasional.
3. Every over-threshold explosion is a rep in the wrong direction. Cross the street. Leave. No ego.
4. Separate walk types (training / decompression / potty) and use different gear for each.
5. Reactivity is not linear. There will be a bad week. Bad weeks are data, not failure.

WEEK 0 (PREP — before the dog is involved)
Order gear. Read the free HSSV Reactive Dog Training Guide. Film two normal walks for baseline + to diagnose fear vs frustration. Register for HSSV Top Dogs L1 (starts Wed 19 Aug, 6:15pm). Map the neighborhood for low-traffic training spots and one open space with sightlines.

WEEK 1 — CHARGE THE MARKER + STOP THE BLEEDING
Goal: dog understands "yes!"=food; you stop rehearsing reactivity.
- Marker charging, 2x/day, 2 min, in the house. Say "yes", feed. 20 reps. No behavior required.
- "Find It" scatter cue, indoors then backyard.
- MANAGEMENT MODE on all walks: cross the street, go behind cars, U-turn early. Do not train reactivity yet. Goal for the week is ZERO reactions, achieved entirely by avoidance.
- Enrichment baseline starts NOW: bowl retired, flirt pole 10 min/day, one long-line sniff walk.

WEEK 2 — U-TURN + FIRST LOOSE-LEASH WORK
- Build the "let's go" U-turn in the house/backyard, then boring streets. Cue, turn, jog 10-20 ft, mark, feed. 20+ reps before you ever need it.
- Track A: 10-min training walks in the most boring place you can find. Feed at your pant seam for correct position. Leash tight = stop moving.
- Still managing, not training, around other dogs.
- Practice "1-2-3 treat" walking pattern.

WEEK 3 — FIND THRESHOLD, START ENGAGE
- Find the actual threshold distance. Park at the edge of a place with dogs (parking lot facing a park). Stay in/near the car. Note the distance where the dog notices but still eats.
- Track B begins: STAGE 1 ENGAGE only. Dog looks at dog → mark → feed. Repeat. 5-10 min max, then leave.
- 2-3 sessions this week. Stationary, from a fixed spot. Not on a walk.
- HSSV Top Dogs L1 starts around here — align if the 19 Aug cohort is the one you took.

WEEK 4 — CONSOLIDATE ENGAGE
- More Engage reps, same distance. Do NOT close distance yet. Boring consistency is the work.
- Track A: extend training walks to 15 min, add one mild distraction.
- Mid-point video: re-film a walk, compare to Week 0 baseline. You will not notice progress day to day; the video will show it.

WEEK 5 — INTRODUCE DISENGAGE
- STAGE 2: dog looks at trigger → silently count to 3 → if they look back at you first, mark and feed jackpot. If not, drop back to Stage 1.
- Only move to Stage 2 when Stage 1 is fluent and relaxed at that distance.
- Start closing distance in SMALL increments — a few feet at a time, and only when the dog is offering disengagement readily.

WEEK 6 — TAKE IT MOBILE
- Move Engage-Disengage from stationary to a slow-moving walk in a moderate-traffic area.
- Keep emergency tools loaded: U-turn, Find It scatter, 1-2-3.
- Expect regression when you add movement. Normal. Drop distance back and rebuild.

WEEK 7 — GENERALIZE
- Same protocol, 3 different locations. Dogs generalize badly; a skill learned in one parking lot is a skill that exists only in that parking lot.
- Vary trigger types: big dogs, small dogs, dogs behind fences, dogs across the street.
- Track A and B start to merge — one walk where you use both sets of skills.

WEEK 8 — ASSESS AND DECIDE
- Re-film. Compare against Week 0 and Week 4.
- Measure the right metric: threshold DISTANCE (has it shrunk?) and RECOVERY TIME (how fast after a reaction does the dog take food again?). Recovery time usually improves before frequency does — it's the leading indicator.
- Decision gate: clear progress → continue + book HSSV Top Dogs L2 in person. Flat → book 2-3 privates with a CBCC-KA / IAABC CDBC trainer. Worse, or any bite → veterinary behaviorist.

THE "I ONLY HAVE 10 MINUTES" VERSION (for bad days — this is the realistic default, not the exception)
Scatter dinner in the grass (2 min) + 10 min flirt pole + skip the walk entirely. A skipped walk is not a failed day. A walk where the dog rehearsed three explosions IS a failed day. Skipping is the better choice and you should feel fine about it.

THE 40-MINUTE VERSION
5 min marker/trick warm-up indoors → 10 min Track A training walk → 20 min decompression long-line sniff walk → 5 min settle with a chew.

tasks.title: Order the equipment (~$110-160)
tasks.description:
Buy before Week 1. Full reasoning is in the 'loose-leash mechanics and equipment' subtask.

THE LIST:
1. FRONT-CLIP / DUAL-CLIP HARNESS — pick ONE:
   - Blue-9 Balance Harness, buckle-neck version, ~$40-50. 6 adjustment points, 2 D-rings. Buckle-neck = doesn't go over the head. Sold via Chewy, Amazon, shop.clickertraining.com.
   - 2 Hounds Design Freedom No-Pull Harness, ~$33-39. Front + back rings, gentle martingale across the chest. 2houndsdesign.com (from $32.98), Mud Bay ($32.99-38.99), Target.
2. DOUBLE-ENDED LEASH, ~$20-30 — DO NOT SKIP THIS. Clips to front AND back ring. It's the power-steering that lets you turn the dog away from a trigger without hauling on their neck. Highest-leverage item on the list and the one people leave out.
3. LONG LINE, 15-30ft, BIOTHANE, ~$25-35. For decompression sniff walks. Not retractable, ever.
4. TREAT POUCH, ~$15. A fumbled treat is a lost rep.
5. HIGH-VALUE FOOD — string cheese, turkey hot dog, chicken, freeze-dried liver. Soft and smelly. Not kibble, not dry biscuits.
6. FLIRT POLE, ~$25 (or DIY from a horse lunge whip + rope + toy). Best effort-to-payoff item for a collie mix.

MEASURE THE DOG'S CHEST GIRTH BEFORE ORDERING — sizing on both harnesses is by chest, not weight.

NOT ON THE LIST, DELIBERATELY: prong collar, choke chain, e-collar. AVSAB's 2021 position statement says there's no role for aversive tools in behavior modification. For a reactive dog specifically these risk teaching 'other dogs = pain', which suppresses the barking while making the underlying emotion worse.

Head halter (Gentle Leader, ~$20-27) is OPTIONAL — only if harness + double leash isn't enough to keep you safe, and only if you'll do the 1-2 week conditioning it needs.

tasks.title: Film two normal walks — baseline video + fear-vs-frustration diagnosis
tasks.description:
Do this BEFORE any training starts. Two jobs in one.

HOW: phone on a gimbal or ask someone to walk alongside filming. Two walks, normal route, normal time of day. Capture at least two encounters with other dogs. Don't stage anything, don't try to make the dog look good or bad.

JOB 1 — BASELINE. You will not perceive progress day to day. In Week 4 and Week 8 you'll re-film and compare. This is the only honest measure you'll have.

JOB 2 — DIAGNOSE WHICH KIND OF REACTIVITY. Matters because prognosis and emphasis differ. Watch the body language in the 3 seconds BEFORE the bark:
- FRUSTRATION type: loose wiggly body, tail high and wagging, whining or squeaking, pulling TOWARD the other dog, straining forward. Translation: 'I want to say hi and this leash won't let me.' Very common in adolescent herding dogs who were friendly off-leash as puppies. Generally faster to resolve.
- FEAR type: body low or stiff/frozen, weight shifted back, hackles up, hard stare, lip licking, whale eye, tries to retreat or get behind you first. Translation: 'make it go away.' Slower, needs more distance, more likely to benefit from professional help.
- Can be a mix. Note which dominates.

ALSO NOTE, and write into this description afterward:
- Roughly how many feet away the dog first notices vs first reacts (your rough threshold distance)
- Whether the dog will take a treat at various distances — this is the practical threshold test
- Whether it's ALL dogs or specific types (big/small/male/behind fences/head-on vs passing)
- How long after a reaction before the dog can take food again (recovery time)

RECORD YOUR ANSWERS HERE. You'll want them when you talk to a trainer, and recovery time is the metric that improves first.

tasks.title: Scout and write down 3 low-traffic training locations
tasks.description:
The plan needs three specific places. Spend a weekend morning finding them and note the actual addresses/names here.

1. BORING SPOT — for Track A leash mechanics. Somewhere with essentially no other dogs. Empty office park at the weekend, quiet cul-de-sac, empty school lot. You need somewhere so dull the dog can focus on you.

2. THRESHOLD SPOT — for Track B reactivity work. Needs LONG SIGHTLINES and a place you can park or stand at the edge with an easy exit. Classic: a parking lot facing a park where dogs come and go 100+ feet away. You must be able to control distance and leave instantly. Being able to work from beside/inside the car early on is a genuine advantage.

3. DECOMPRESSION SPOT — open low-traffic space for long-line sniff walks. Regional park at off-peak hours, quiet trail.

ALSO CONSIDER: Sniffspot (sniffspot.com) rents private fenced yards by the hour. Genuinely useful for reactive dogs — you get space with zero other dogs. Worth checking what's available near you and noting prices here.

TIMING NOTE: 6pm on a neighborhood sidewalk is the highest-trigger, lowest-benefit hour of the day. Since you're limited to evenings and weekends, being willing to DRIVE 10 minutes to a quiet spot is worth more than any piece of equipment on the list.
